title: Spies Before Spy Agencies
description: Sun Tzu's five kinds of spy, the Arthashastra's fake holy men and Rome's grain officers turned informers

concepts.title: Sun Tzu: Knowledge from Other Men
concepts.contentHtml:
Long before anyone founded a secret service, rulers were writing manuals on how to run spies. The most famous is the Chinese classic The Art of War, traditionally credited to Sun Tzu. You may have met its ideas on deception in Military History. Its thirteenth and final chapter, "The Use of Spies", is a practical handbook for the people who do the finding out.

The argument starts with money. An army of a hundred thousand drains the state every day, and a war can drag on for years before a single day decides it, so refusing to spend a little silver on spies is, in Lionel Giles's translation, "the height of inhumanity". What wins wars is foreknowledge, and the text is blunt about where it comes from. It cannot be drawn from spirits, or worked out from experience or calculation: knowledge of the enemy's dispositions can only be obtained from other men.1

Sun Tzu then names five classes of spy:

  • Local spies: inhabitants of the district.
  • Inward spies: officials serving the enemy.
  • Converted spies: the enemy's own spies, found, bribed and turned.
  • Doomed spies: your own agents, allowed to learn false information so that they will carry it to the enemy.
  • Surviving spies: those who go and come back with news.

The converted spy is the keystone. Through him you recruit local and inward spies, send the doomed spy off with false tidings and time the surviving spy's missions, so the text insists he be treated with the utmost generosity. Notice what this is: a theory of the double agent, written down in ancient China, and the same idea that Britain would turn into a war-winning system in the Second World War (lesson 5). The chapter is ruthless too. A spy who leaks a secret before the time is ripe must be put to death, together with the man he told.

concepts.title: The Arthashastra: Holy Men on the Payroll
concepts.contentHtml:
In India the Arthashastra, a Sanskrit treatise on statecraft, goes further still. Tradition credits it to Kautilya (also called Chanakya), adviser to the founder of the Mauryan Empire, Chandragupta, in the 4th century BCE, though that authorship has been challenged. The work was known only from later references until the Sanskrit scholar Rudrapatna Shamasastry found a copy in 1905.1 His English translation of 1915 brought it to readers worldwide.

Its chapter "The Institution of Spies" reads like a staff list. The king creates spies in nine guises: a fraudulent disciple, a recluse, a householder, a merchant, an ascetic, a classmate, a fire-brand, a poisoner and a mendicant woman. Several of them run whole cover businesses. The recluse is given land, money and disciples to farm and trade; out of the profits he feeds other ascetics, sends them out to detect crimes against the king's wealth, and collects their reports when they come for their wages.

The fake holy man is the best part. He settles outside a city with a band of disciples with shaved heads or braided hair, and pretends to live on a handful of vegetables or meadow grass, eaten once every month or two. In private he may eat his favourite foods. His disciples spread word of his supernatural powers. When people come to learn their future, he "foretells" what his disciples have signalled to him by nods and signs, and the king's minister then makes the prophecies come true, rewarding some and secretly punishing those found plotting.

Two lessons stand out. First, the cover is a real job, paid for by the state. Second, the main target is often not a foreign army but the king's own household: these networks exist to test the loyalty of the king's servants. Elsewhere the book sends spies abroad in the guise of ordinary trades, and it counts women among the most effective agents.

concepts.title: Rome's Grain Officers Turn Informers
concepts.contentHtml:
Rome's spies hid inside its supply system. The frumentarii (from frumentum, grain) were at first junior officers attached to the army's commissary, the service that kept soldiers fed. Probably under Trajan, around the turn of the second century CE, they became couriers carrying military dispatches.1 Many were then attached to the imperial service as what one modern editor calls "a sort of secret police". A courier who travels everywhere and carries the emperor's letters is perfectly placed to listen.

Trajan's successor Hadrian is the emperor we see using them most clearly. His biography in the Historia Augusta says his vigilance reached into his friends' households, and it tells a story to show how much he found out. A man's wife wrote to him complaining that he was so taken up with pleasures and baths that he would not come home. Hadrian's agents learned of the letter. When the husband asked for a furlough, Hadrian reproached him with his baths and his pleasures. The man's reply has the ring of real alarm: "What, did my wife write you just what she wrote to me?"

Read that story with care. The Historia Augusta is a later collection of imperial lives, and like much ancient biography it mixes record with gossip. It is better evidence of what Romans believed about the emperor's agents than of what any one agent did. The same biography lists the habit among Hadrian's faults, which tells you how the system felt to those it watched: an emperor who reads his officials' family letters rules them partly through fear.

Put the three traditions side by side and the jobs of every later service are already visible: gather secrets abroad, watch for disloyalty at home, and deceive. The rest of this topic follows those three jobs from Tudor England to the Cold War.

title: Walsingham's Web
description: Elizabeth I's spymaster, a double agent, a beer barrel and the trap that convicted Mary, Queen of Scots

concepts.title: Elizabeth's Spymaster
concepts.contentHtml:
Elizabeth I ruled a Protestant kingdom surrounded by Catholic enemies. After the pope excommunicated her in 1570, plots to kill her and crown a Catholic in her place were a constant danger, and the obvious candidate was her cousin Mary, Queen of Scots, who had fled to England in 1568 and was held there under guard. Elizabeth's chief minister William Cecil, Lord Burghley, built much of his power on a highly effective intelligence service run by Sir Francis Walsingham, the queen's principal secretary.

Walsingham had no agency in the modern sense: no headquarters, no budget line, no badge. He had people. By one account he raised the number of English spies to more than fifty, recruited many at Oxford and Cambridge, and paid a good number of them out of his own income. He died in debt in 1590. His agents ranged from couriers and informers to double agents among English Catholics. Some are glimpsed only in passing in the state papers. Thomas Cely, one of Elizabeth's Yeomen of the Guard and most probably also a spy, wrote to her in 1579 as a galley slave of the Spanish Inquisition, after being put to the rack.1

You met one side of this world in Lost Scripts & Decipherment: the ciphers Mary used and the codebreakers who read them. That is real, but it can mislead. Codebreaking only works if you can get hold of the letters, and getting hold of them is a human problem. Walsingham's real talent was for placing people, and sometimes for letting a plot grow until it could be used. A popular picture has Mary undone by a brilliant feat of cryptography. The evidence in the next concept shows something closer to a sting operation, with the codebreaker as one member of the team.

concepts.title: The Beer-Barrel Post
concepts.contentHtml:
In spring 1586 a young Catholic gentleman, Anthony Babington, was recruited into a plot. With Spanish support, a rebellion would break out at the same moment as Elizabeth's assassination, and Mary would be crowned in her place. Walsingham learned of the conspiracy from one of his double agents, and instead of crushing it he saw an opportunity.

Mary was then held at Chartley Hall in Staffordshire, always under guard. Walsingham gave her a way out that he controlled. His agent Gilbert Gifford, pretending to sympathise with her cause, offered to carry letters between Mary and her supporters. They would travel hidden in the beer barrels delivered to her household. Mary agreed, believing her post was finally safe.

Every letter was intercepted. Walsingham's cryptographer Thomas Phelippes unsealed it, deciphered it and reported its contents, and it was then resealed and sent on as if nothing had happened. In this way Walsingham read all of Mary's correspondence.1 Meanwhile Gifford befriended the English Catholics in the plot and encouraged them to go on with their plans.

On 17 July 1586 Mary dictated the letter that would kill her. Now known as the "Gallows Letter", it replied to Babington, approved the plan and agreed to Elizabeth's murder, telling him to "sett the six gentlemen to woork". The six were the men who would kill the queen. When Phelippes had deciphered it, he drew a gallows on the address leaf, a grim little sketch of what its contents meant for the writer.

Notice the structure. The channel was Walsingham's from the start, so Mary's caution counted for nothing: she encrypted carefully and handed the result to her enemy's courier. A cipher protects a message's content, not its route, and no cipher can protect you from a messenger who works for the other side.

concepts.title: Entrapment and Its Afterlife
concepts.contentHtml:
Walsingham wanted more than Mary's consent; he wanted names. Before her letter went on to Babington, he had several passages amended and a forged postscript added, asking Babington to name the six assassins and to say how he was proceeding. Nothing came back. On 3 August he ordered Babington's arrest, and the same day he wrote to Phelippes that he feared the postscript had "bread the iealousie", that is, aroused suspicion. Babington hid for some days in St John's Wood before he was caught. Mary's secretaries confessed to writing the letter at her command, and Babington was hanged, drawn and quartered on 20 September 1586. Mary was tried on 14 October 1586 and executed on 8 February 1587.

Was this justice or entrapment? Both readings have support.

  • Against Mary: the plot was not Walsingham's invention, the assassination was approved in her own dictated words, and her secretaries confirmed it.
  • Against Walsingham: he opened the channel, his agent urged the plotters on, and he doctored the very letter used as evidence.

Historians still weigh these differently, but they agree that the case was built by agents and informers as much as by codebreaking.

The same world produced a famous death. On 30 May 1593 the playwright Christopher Marlowe was stabbed in a house in Deptford. The coroner's papers, found only in 1925, show he was in the company of Robert Poley and Nicholas Skeres, experienced agents who had helped uncover the Babington Plot.1 Marlowe himself had worked for the queen's service: in 1587 the Privy Council assured Cambridge that he had done "her majesty good service". Whether his death was a brawl over the bill or something darker is still argued.

title: Spies of the American Revolution
description: Nathan Hale's doomed mission, the Culper Ring, invisible ink and a codebook in almost alphabetical order

concepts.title: Nathan Hale: The Spy Who Was Caught
concepts.contentHtml:
In August 1776 the Continental Army lost the fighting at Brooklyn Heights and fell back into Manhattan, and George Washington badly needed to know what the British would do next. Lieutenant Colonel Thomas Knowlton asked his Rangers for a volunteer to cross the lines in disguise. His men were willing to die in battle but not to die in disguise. Only one man answered: Nathan Hale, a 21-year-old Yale graduate who had been a schoolteacher. He reportedly told a classmate that every kind of service necessary to the public good becomes honourable by being necessary.

On the night of 15 September 1776 Hale set off for Long Island dressed as a schoolmaster looking for work, carrying his Yale diploma as proof. He had no training, no network and no safe way to send reports back. Details of his mission and capture are scant. He was hanged on 22 September 1776, just one day after his capture. At the time, spies were not treated as prisoners of war; they were hanged as illegal combatants.

Then there are the famous last words: "I only regret that I have but one life to lose for my country." Generations of American schoolchildren have learned them. Witness accounts agree that he met his death with composure and a firm resolve, but no contemporary source confirms that he spoke those words.1 Hale's real importance is what he taught Washington. A lone amateur with a cover story was not an intelligence system.

Hale's afterlife has been long. There is no known portrait of him, so the sculptor Bela Lyon Pratt used a local man of the same age as a model for the statue at Yale. A replica was unveiled at CIA headquarters on 6 June 1973, and officers about to leave for an assignment keep a tradition of placing a quarter, which bears Washington's face, around it for luck.

concepts.title: The Culper Ring
concepts.contentHtml:
When the British made New York their headquarters again in 1778, Washington built something better than a lone volunteer: a standing network. He put it in the hands of Major Benjamin Tallmadge, who had once lived in Brookhaven on Long Island and used the alias John Bolton. Tallmadge recruited friends and neighbours from Setauket, people whose movements nobody would question.

The chain worked like a relay:

  • Robert Townsend ("Samuel Culper, Junior"), a Quaker merchant, gathered news in Manhattan, mingling with British officers through a dry-goods shop and Rivington's coffee house.
  • Austin Roe, a tavern keeper, carried it out of the city on the pretext of buying supplies and buried it in a meadow.
  • Abraham Woodhull ("Samuel Culper"), a farmer, collected it and passed it to Caleb Brewster, who took it by whaleboat across Long Island Sound to Connecticut.
  • Dragoons then rode Tallmadge's packets to Washington.

In the story as usually told, Anna Strong signalled to Woodhull with a black petticoat on her washing line, while the number of handkerchiefs beside it showed which cove Brewster was waiting in. The route from Manhattan to Setauket alone was fifty miles, so the news was often slow. But it was steady, and in summer 1779 Culper Junior warned of an attack planned on the French army at Newport, Rhode Island.

Secrecy was extreme even by later standards. Washington never met either Culper.1 Townsend made Woodhull promise never to reveal his identity, and the secret held for 160 years: Culper Junior was identified only in 1939, when the Long Island historian Morton Pennypacker noticed that his handwriting matched Robert Townsend's.

concepts.title: Codes, Stains and Tradecraft
concepts.contentHtml:
In July 1779 Tallmadge gave the ring a code, built on John Entick's dictionary, and made only four copies of the codebook. Common words got numbers, and so did names: 711 meant Washington, 712 the British commander Clinton, 721 John Bolton, 722 Culper and 723 Culper Junior. It had a fatal-looking flaw. Tallmadge numbered the words in nearly alphabetical order (they 629, there 630, thing 631), so low numbers meant words near the start of the alphabet. Anyone with a few decoded words could have guessed the rest. The code could have been easily broken, but it never was.1

The ring's real protection was concealment. The brothers James and John Jay had developed an invisible ink they called the "stain" or "white ink", whose exact recipe is still unknown. Writing in it vanished on the page and reappeared only when brushed with a "sympathetic" developer. In September 1779 Washington told Tallmadge how to use it well: write on the blank leaves of pamphlets, almanacs, registers or cheap books, because British searches were aimed mainly at paper folded up like letters. Agents also wrote between the lines of ordinary private letters.

The danger was real. In April 1779 Woodhull was writing a secret report, with British officers lodged next door, when two female relatives burst into his room; the fright left him in poor health for a long time afterwards. In May 1781 British sentries searched him at the Brooklyn ferry because "some villain" was carrying messages out of the city.

The same war shows what happened to spies who failed. In September 1780 the British officer John André, who coordinated British intelligence and had been dealing with the traitor Benedict Arnold, was caught out of uniform with plans of West Point hidden in his boot. Washington had him hanged on 2 October 1780, four years after Hale.

title: The First Modern Secret Services
description: Spy fever, the Secret Service Bureau of 1909, lemon-juice ink, cigar codes and the real Mata Hari

concepts.title: Spy Fever and the Bureau of 1909
concepts.contentHtml:
Until the twentieth century, Britain's intelligence was gathered mostly by branches of the army and navy, with no permanent civilian service. That changed in an atmosphere close to panic. In the years before 1914 the press and popular novels filled readers with fear of a German invasion helped by secret agents on British soil. The books of William Le Queux, master of the invasion-scare spy novel, sold in huge numbers and fed what one historian calls a "quasi-collective psychosis".

In 1909 a committee of imperial defence, expecting a possible war with Germany, set up the Secret Service Bureau. Within a year, in 1910, it split in two:

  • A home section under the army officer Vernon Kell, known as "K", to find German spies in Britain. It became the Security Service, MI5.
  • A foreign section under the naval officer Mansfield Smith-Cumming, known as "C", to gather intelligence abroad. It became the Secret Intelligence Service, MI6, whose chiefs have been known as "C" ever since.

The letters MI simply stand for military intelligence. The home section had no police powers, so it relied on police forces such as Special Branch to make arrests.

How do historians know any of this? Unevenly. MI5 has released many of its old files to The National Archives at Kew, where anyone can read them. MI6 has not: confusingly, the archive's own guide notes that no records generated by the agency are held there.1 Its early history is known chiefly through an authorised history by Keith Jeffery covering 1909 to 1949, and through what other departments recorded.

concepts.title: Catching Spies in the Great War
concepts.contentHtml:
German spying in Britain during the First World War was unsophisticated. Many agents were recruited off the streets, given basic training and sent to report by post or telegram. That was their weakness, because Britain built large censorship departments that read letters and telegrams going abroad, and a laboratory that tested suspicious letters for invisible ink.

Two cases show how they were caught. In May 1915 Haicke Janssen and Willem Roos, Dutch sailors posing as travelling cigar salesmen, toured naval ports and telegraphed orders to an address in Holland. Their price list was a code in which each cigar type meant a kind of warship, so when Roos ordered 10,000 Sumatra cigars from Edinburgh, he meant that ten battleships were in port there.1 Censors found the telegrams suspicious, and both men were arrested and shot at the Tower of London.

Carl Muller, a German posing as a Russian, wrote reports between the lines of innocent letters in lemon juice. The censors passed a warm iron over one and the writing appeared. When he was arrested, a lemon was found in his dressing-table drawer; he claimed it was for his teeth. He too was executed at the Tower. MI5 then kept sending messages in his name and asked the Germans for more money. They sent it, and MI5 bought a car that it christened "The Muller", earning a reprimand from the Treasury. The shrivelled lemon is still in the archive.

How good was MI5 really? Speaking for The National Archives, the intelligence historian Gill Bennett calls it extremely successful at detecting German spies, and the archive's experts see the Muller trick as a forerunner of the Second World War's double-cross system. The historian Emmanuel Debruyne is more sceptical: he argues MI5's effectiveness from the outbreak of war is mainly a myth, since it identified only a minority of German agents and the rest failed chiefly because their links to Germany broke down. Eleven spies were executed in Britain between November 1914 and April 1916.

concepts.title: Mata Hari: The Legend and the File
concepts.contentHtml:
No spy of the First World War is more famous than Mata Hari, and few are less understood. She was born Margaretha Zelle in Leeuwarden in the Netherlands in 1876, married an army officer in the Dutch East Indies, and after her divorce reinvented herself in Paris as an exotic dancer. Her stage name came from a Javanese term for the sun, "the day's eye". She invented romantic origins for herself and acquired a long list of lovers, some of them senior officers.

The documented espionage is thin. When the war ruined her career, the German consul in The Hague offered her money to gather information in France, and she accepted, becoming agent H21. In September 1916 Captain Georges Ladoux of French intelligence proposed that she work as a double agent for France. Her reports proved of little interest or out of date, and in January 1917 Ladoux refused to pay her. She was arrested in Paris in February 1917, after French intelligence obtained German messages about H21.

Her trial came at a dark moment for France, after the costly defeat at the Chemin des Dames. She was convicted and shot at Vincennes on 15 October 1917. Afterwards she was held responsible for the deaths of 50,000 Allied soldiers and portrayed as a seductress who traded sex for secrets.1 Historians such as Julie Wheelwright argue that she was a useful scapegoat: a foreign, independent woman who made a convenient culprit at a time of heavy losses.

A fair verdict sits between the legends. She did take German money and a German code name, so she was not simply an innocent dancer. But there is little evidence that she passed anything of value, the case against her rested on circumstantial and partly manufactured evidence, and the 50,000 deaths are propaganda, not a finding. In a final twist, Ladoux himself was soon arrested on espionage charges.

title: Double Cross and D-Day
description: Turned German agents, Garbo's imaginary network, a corpse with false papers and the great deception of D-Day

concepts.title: The Double Cross System
concepts.contentHtml:
In the Second World War Britain did what Sun Tzu had recommended: it turned the enemy's spies. MI5 captured almost all of the German agents sent to Britain, often on arrival. Many were taken to Camp 020 at Latchmere House on Ham Common for interrogation by Captain Robin "Tin Eye" Stephens, a fierce figure with a monocle. He used psychological pressure (prisoners made to stand, shouted at, deprived of sleep) but forbade physical violence because he believed it did not work.

Those who seemed usable were offered a choice. In January 1941 a Twenty Committee was set up to coordinate the growing number of double agents. The name was a joke: XX is twenty in Roman numerals and also a double cross. Its chairman, the Oxford historian John Masterman, later summed up the result: MI5 "actively ran and controlled the German espionage system" in Britain.

Running a double agent is delicate. He must send enough genuine but harmless information, called chicken feed, to keep his German controllers' trust. Codebreakers at Bletchley Park (History of Technology tells their story) could read German intelligence signals, so MI5 could check what the Germans believed and what they still did not know.

The longest-serving wireless double agent was Tate, the Danish-born Wulf Schmidt, who parachuted into England in September 1940 and was quickly caught. His German handlers trusted him completely, awarded him the Iron Cross and called him "a pearl". His false reports of a minefield south of Ireland kept U-boats away from an important convoy route, and late in the war he misreported where flying bombs were landing so that the Germans changed their aim and fewer landed in built-up areas. He settled in Watford after the war as Harry Williamson.

A myth worth dropping: not every captured spy was turned. Some were unsuitable and were executed, and one of them, Josef Jakobs, was the last person executed at the Tower of London.1

concepts.title: Garbo and Fortitude
concepts.contentHtml:
The most valuable double agent began as a fantasist. In January 1941 Juan Pujol García, a Spaniard who hated fascism and had trained at Spain's Royal Poultry School, offered to spy for Britain and was refused. He then offered himself to the Germans, who told him to get to England and send a report. He got only as far as Lisbon.1 There he started inventing "intelligence" from public sources, credited to a network of imaginary sub-agents. It contained mistakes, since he had never seen Britain, but the Germans began paying him.

British codebreakers read the German messages about him, and by February 1942 the British had identified him and recruited him. Codenamed Garbo for his star quality, he and his MI5 case officer, Tomás Harris, built a fictional network of some 26 sub-agents by June 1944, producing a stream of hundreds of messages. Not one of the sub-agents existed.

Garbo became central to Operation Fortitude South, the effort to convince Germany that the main invasion would come at the Pas de Calais rather than Normandy. It invented the First US Army Group, an imaginary force in south-east England built from fake radio traffic, inflatable tanks and dummy landing craft, which double agents then confirmed. On the night before D-Day, dummy parachutists nicknamed "Ruperts" were dropped behind the German lines, and on the morning of 6 June 1944 aircraft scattered strips of foil called Window to fake two invasion fleets on German radar.

Three days later Garbo sent his masterstroke: Normandy was a diversion, and the main assault was still to come in the Pas de Calais. The Germans believed as late as July 1944 that a second, larger invasion would land near Calais, and kept forces waiting for it. That July his German handlers told him he had been awarded the Iron Cross; Britain also made him an MBE. After the war he vanished until the writer Nigel West traced him to Venezuela and met him in New Orleans in 1984.

concepts.title: Operation Mincemeat
concepts.contentHtml:
Early in the war, Admiral John Godfrey's naval intelligence division circulated a list of deception ideas, probably drafted by his assistant Ian Fleming, later the creator of James Bond. Number 28 was letting the Germans find a corpse carrying false plans, noted as "A suggestion. (not a very nice one.)" Fleming admitted he had taken the idea from a 1937 novel by a former head of Scotland Yard's detectives.

In 1943 the Allies' next target, Sicily, was obvious, so Ewen Montagu of naval intelligence and Charles Cholmondeley, an RAF officer seconded to MI5, turned the idea into Operation Mincemeat. They needed a body that would look drowned. They found Glyndwr Michael, a homeless Welshman who died in London on 24 January 1943 after swallowing rat poison. He became "Major William Martin" of the Royal Marines, carrying a letter from a senior British general that pointed to landings in Greece and Sardinia. His pockets held carefully built pocket litter: love letters and a photograph of his fiancée "Pam" (really MI5 secretary Jean Leslie), theatre ticket stubs, a tailor's bill and a receipt for an engagement ring.

The submarine HMS Seraph released the body off Huelva in Spain, where the currents ran towards shore and German agents were active. The body of Major Martin was found at around 9:30am on 30 April 1943 by a local fisherman. German agents photographed the papers. By the end of June German forces on Sardinia had doubled to 10,000, and divisions were moving to Greece and the Balkans. Even four hours after the invasion of Sicily began on 9 July, 21 Axis aircraft left Sicily to reinforce Sardinia.1

Why did it work so well? Partly because it told the enemy what many already suspected: much of the Italian high command thought Sicily too obvious and expected Sardinia. Good deception confirms an existing belief rather than creating a new one. Michael's true identity was added to his grave in Huelva only in 1997.

title: Atomic Spies and the Cambridge Five
description: Venona's flawed one-time pads, the atomic spies, the Rosenberg debate and Britain's Cambridge moles

concepts.title: Venona: Reading Moscow's Old Mail
concepts.contentHtml:
During the Second World War, Soviet intelligence officers in the United States sent their reports to Moscow by telegraph cable, and the US government simply collected copies. Reading them should have been impossible, because they were encrypted with a one-time pad, the system Number Stations explains: if every page of random key is used once and only once, the cipher cannot be broken.

On 1 February 1943 the US Army's Signal Intelligence Service began the secret Venona project at Arlington Hall, a former girls' school in Virginia. In autumn 1943 Lieutenant Richard Hallock, an archaeologist turned codebreaker, found evidence of duplicate key pages. The popular story blames lazy Soviet clerks for reusing pads. The truth is stranger. For a few months in early 1942, a time of great strain for the Soviet regime, the KGB's own cryptographic centre printed duplicate copies of the key on more than 35,000 pages and bound them into separate pads, so supposedly unique pages existed twice.1

Exploiting that slip took years. The linguist Meredith Gardner first broke into the messages in December 1946; by 1948 the FBI had joined, and more than 2,900 Soviet telegrams were eventually read in whole or part. Every spy had a codename, so the decrypts still had to be matched to people. Sometimes the senders were careless. One message gave the wife of the agent ANTENNA (later LIBERAL) her real name, Ethel. Another agent was MLAD, Russian for "youngster"; Theodore Hall was only 19 when he began spying.

Venona had limits. Only messages up to about 1945 were vulnerable, and the secret was too valuable to reveal in court, so the government could not use it as evidence. Moscow learned of the project in 1949 through its British agent Kim Philby. The programme ended on 1 October 1980, and its existence was officially confirmed only in 1995.

concepts.title: The Atomic Spies and the Rosenberg Debate
concepts.contentHtml:
Experts expected the Soviet Union to need years to build an atomic bomb, yet it tested one on 29 August 1949. Espionage was part of the reason. Venona and the investigations it started exposed several spies inside the Manhattan Project, which the 20th Century topic covers.

The most important was Klaus Fuchs, a German-born physicist and communist who fled the Nazis to Britain in 1933, joined the British bomb project and became a British citizen in 1942. He passed secrets first to Soviet military intelligence and then through the courier Harry Gold, and at Los Alamos he worked on the implosion design of the "Fat Man" bomb. Some experts estimate that his information let the Soviets test their bomb one to two years earlier than they otherwise would have. Venona revealed him in 1949; he confessed and was sentenced in 1950 to 14 years.

Theodore Hall, the youngest scientist recruited to Los Alamos, walked into the Communist Party's New York office in October 1944 to offer bomb secrets. He too passed information on the implosion bomb. Hall was never charged with espionage. He moved to Britain, did research in biology at Cambridge, and died there in 1999.

The famous executions were of Julius and Ethel Rosenberg. Venona confirms that Julius (LIBERAL) led a productive spy ring, though the decrypts suggest his main work was military and industrial espionage rather than atomic secrets.1 Ethel's case is harder. Her brother David Greenglass testified that she typed the notes Julius passed on, but before a grand jury in 1950 he had sworn that he never spoke to his sister about it, and he later said he implicated her to protect his own wife. The Rosenbergs were executed on 19 June 1953, the only American civilians executed for espionage in the Cold War. Julius's guilt as a spy is now well established; whether Ethel deserved to die, or was even an active spy, is still argued.

concepts.title: The Cambridge Five
concepts.contentHtml:
In the 1930s Soviet intelligence recruited a group of idealistic young men from Cambridge University who hoped for careers in government. They are now called the Cambridge Five: Kim Philby, Donald Maclean, Guy Burgess, Anthony Blunt and John Cairncross. Between them they penetrated all the major institutions of British state security, from the Foreign Office to MI5 and MI6, and passed secrets for decades.

The damage was measured in lives. In 1945 Konstantin Volkov, a Soviet intelligence officer in Istanbul, offered to defect to the British in return for asylum and money, and warned that Soviet agents held key positions in Britain. The case reached Philby. He tipped off Moscow, and Volkov and his wife were kidnapped, drugged, taken to Moscow, interrogated and executed.1

Venona began the unravelling. A source codenamed HOMER had passed information from the British embassy in Washington in 1944 and 1945, and HOMER was eventually identified as Maclean. In the early 1950s Burgess and Maclean fled to Moscow. Philby fell under suspicion and was dismissed from MI6 but not prosecuted. Confronted by an MI6 officer in Beirut, he gave only a partial confession, and in 1963 he defected to Moscow.

Here is a myth to drop. The neat label "Cambridge Five" came later. At the time MI5 did not know how many there were, and the fear of further moles drove years of searching, a joint MI5 and MI6 review of past cases called the Fluency Committee, and a lasting tightening of vetting.

Our knowledge keeps growing. On 14 January 2025 The National Archives released MI5 files with new details of the cases of Philby, Blunt and Cairncross, including their confessions and the Volkov affair. Each release lets historians test the memoirs and legends against what the watchers actually wrote at the time.

title: Moles, Machines and the Limits of Knowing
description: The Berlin tunnel and George Blake, Gordievsky's escape, hollow coins, spy satellites and ignored warnings

concepts.title: The Tunnel, the Mole and the Escape
concepts.contentHtml:
In the early 1950s almost all Soviet military telephone and telegraph traffic between Moscow, Warsaw and Bucharest passed through Berlin, partly on buried cables. In January 1954 CIA Director Allen Dulles approved a joint plan with MI6 to dig under the border and tap them. Behind the cover of a US radar site, tunnellers removed 3,100 tons of soil; the finished tunnel was 1,476 feet long. British technicians installed the taps, and collection began in May 1955. In under a year it filled 50,000 reels of tape, with 443,000 fully transcribed conversations.

The KGB had known all along. George Blake, an MI6 officer turned Soviet agent, had passed on the plans while the operation was still being designed. To protect him, the KGB let the taps run until April 1956 and then staged an "accidental" discovery. Did it feed the West disinformation in the meantime? Soviet propaganda implied so, but later CIA studies concluded the intelligence was genuine.1 That makes sense: to feed false traffic, the KGB would have had to warn the Soviet and East German users of the lines, and every extra person told was a risk to Blake. Blake was exposed in 1961, confessed after a long interrogation and later escaped from prison.

The Cold War's best-known escape ran the other way. Oleg Gordievsky, a KGB officer recruited by MI6 in Copenhagen, was posted to London in 1982 and gave MI6 the largest haul of intelligence in its history, including the Kremlin's fear of a Western surprise attack. In 1985 he was betrayed by Aldrich Ames, a CIA officer secretly working for the KGB, and recalled to Moscow for a brutal interrogation. He signalled for rescue, and MI6 launched Operation Pimlico, a plan rehearsed for years. On 21 July, after a journey that began two days earlier, he crossed into Finland hidden in a car boot under a heat-shielding blanket meant to defeat sniffer dogs. Over the border, the music on the car's cassette player changed to Sibelius's Finlandia, the sign that he was safe.

concepts.title: Hollow Coins and Eyes in the Sky
concepts.contentHtml:
Spy gadgets look like fiction, but the courts recorded them. In 1953 a hollow nickel was found holding a piece of microfilm with ten columns and 21 rows of five-figure groups, and handed to the FBI. Government codebreakers could not read it. The key arrived only in 1957, when Reino Hayhanen, assistant to the Soviet spy known as Rudolf Abel, defected. Hayhanen became the government's main witness, and the items seized from Abel included a hollowed-out pencil holding microfilms and a block of wood wrapped in sandpaper that hid a cipher pad. In February 1962 Abel was exchanged in Berlin for two Americans, one of them the pilot Francis Gary Powers.

Powers flew the U-2, a spy plane built to photograph the Soviet Union from very high altitude. The first U-2 flight over the USSR was on 4 July 1956. Between 1956 and 1960, 24 missions over the Soviet Union opened a crack in its secrecy, but not one ICBM base was found. On 1 May 1960 a missile brought Powers down near Sverdlovsk, and overflights stopped.

The replacement was in orbit. Corona, disguised as a scientific programme called Discoverer, launched cameras into space and dropped the exposed film back by parachute, where aircraft snagged the capsule in midair over the Pacific. The first 13 missions failed. On 18 August 1960 Mission XIV worked, and it returned more photographic coverage of the Soviet Union than all previous U-2 missions combined.1

The pictures overturned a belief that had shaped American politics. US estimates had warned of a "missile gap" in Moscow's favour. Within months Corona showed that the Soviets were in fact significantly behind the US in developing a workable ICBM. Over its life Corona collected more than 800,000 images, and satellite imagery later made arms-control treaties checkable.

concepts.title: Why Warnings Fail
concepts.contentHtml:
Spies and satellites gather facts; someone still has to believe them. Two disasters of 1941 show how hard that is. Stalin received multiple, detailed and timely warnings of Hitler's invasion of June 1941, from open sources and secret agents alike. He interpreted them on a not-so-bad hypothesis: Hitler would surely issue an ultimatum first and would not risk a two-front war. German deception reinforced the error, and Stalin distrusted secret reports as possible enemy plants. His military intelligence chief even proposed watching mutton prices in occupied Europe, reasoning that a winter campaign needed sheepskin coats; Hitler, expecting a quick victory, prepared no winter campaign. The failure was one of analysis, not collection.1

Pearl Harbor looks different but rhymes. American codebreakers had cracked the Japanese diplomatic cipher PURPLE in 1940, yet Japan's navy used other codes and its carrier force sailed in radio silence. Days before the attack, navy analysts in Hawaii reported that they did not know where four Japanese carriers were. In 1962 the historian Roberta Wohlstetter argued that the US failed to anticipate Pearl Harbor not for lack of relevant information but because of a mass of irrelevant information: real signals were buried in noise, and it is easy to sort them only afterwards. As the political scientist Robert Jervis put it, intelligence is a game between hiders and finders, and the hiders usually have the easier job.

Moscow drew its own lesson from 1941, and overcorrected. From 1981 the KGB's Operation RYAN hunted for signs of a coming American nuclear attack using a deliberate worst-case method. Its London station was told to watch prices at blood banks, which would supposedly rise before a war; British donors are not paid. During the NATO exercise Able Archer 83, Moscow wrongly told its stations that US forces had gone on alert. Some analysts dismissed the scare as Soviet theatre, but evidence from Gordievsky and others suggests it was genuine fear. Expectations, too rosy or too dark, are the hardest thing for any intelligence service to see past.
